standard.title: International law and policy
standard.description: how Australia's international legal obligations shape Australian law and government policies, including those relating to First Nations Australians, and the issues related to the application of these obligations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know how individuals and groups participate in civic life and contribute to global citizenship (AC9HC9K05). They understand the court system's role in applying law (AC9HC9K03, AC9HC9K04).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how Australia's international legal obligations shape Australian law and government policies, including those relating to First Nations Australians, and analyse issues related to applying those obligations.

nodes.label: Australia's key international treaty commitments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the key international treaties Australia has signed and ratified, and explain what signing and ratifying a treaty requires of the Australian Government.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two international treaties Australia has signed and ratified, and explain the difference between signing and ratifying a treaty.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the main categories of international human rights and other treaties Australia has signed and ratified, explain the signing-to-ratification-to-implementation pathway, and describe what these obligations require of the Australian Government.
wider: Research how many of the 9 key UN human rights treaties Australia has signed and ratified, and identify any that Australia has signed but not ratified
Investigate the reservations Australia has entered on certain treaty obligations and what this means for compliance
Examine the role of the UN treaty monitoring bodies and how Australia has engaged with them
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand the signing-ratification-implementation distinction will not be able to analyse the gap between Australia's stated obligations and its actual policies — they lack the conceptual framework to identify issues in application.

response_modes.reason: The treaty pathway (signed → ratified → implemented) is not self-evident and students frequently conflate stages. Invest in this foundational concept before examining specific treaty effects on domestic law.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two international treaties Australia has signed and ratified
Explains the difference between signing and ratifying a treaty
Describes at least one obligation that ratification creates for the Australian Government

nodes.label: How international obligations shape domestic law and policy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how at least one international convention or declaration has shaped Australian law or government policy, using specific examples.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how at least one international convention or declaration has shaped a specific Australian law or government policy, using an example.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how international conventions and declarations — including the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, the Paris Agreement, the World Heritage Convention, and the Refugee Convention — have shaped Australian law and government policies, with specific examples for at least two.
wider: Trace in detail how the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples has shaped (or not shaped) Australian government law and policies with respect to First Nations Australians
Analyse Australia's legal obligations under the Paris Agreement (2016) and evaluate the extent to which Australian policy meets those obligations
Investigate how the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and its protocol shape Australia's offshore processing policy, and analyse the issues this creates
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot connect specific treaties to specific policy changes cannot complete the 'issues in application' analysis that is the descriptor's second key demand — they need the treaty-to-policy link established before they can examine where it breaks down.

response_modes.reason: Covering at least two distinct treaty-policy examples (e.g. UNDRIP and climate, or climate and refugees) gives students a comparative base — they see that different obligations create different kinds of issues rather than treating all treaties as equivalent.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The UNDRIP-First Nations pathway is rich because students can trace an ongoing, contested relationship between international obligation and domestic policy — it is not a resolved case. Similarly, the refugee convention and offshore processing is a live controversy connecting international law to contested domestic policy.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one international convention or declaration and the obligation it creates
Explains how that obligation has shaped a specific Australian law or government policy
Uses accurate examples with correct names of treaties and policies

nodes.label: Issues in applying international obligations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse issues related to Australia's application of its international legal obligations, including tensions between international and domestic law, political will, and enforcement.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one issue or tension in Australia's application of an international legal obligation and provide a basic explanation of why the issue arises.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse issues related to the application of Australia's international obligations, including: the gap between ratified obligations and domestic implementation, tensions between international law and domestic political interests, and the limits of international enforcement mechanisms.
wider: Evaluate the impact of international obligations on First Nations Australians' reconciliation, truth-telling and sovereignty claims, and assess whether Australia's application of relevant instruments is adequate
Compare cases where Australia has been found non-compliant with international obligations and assess the consequences
Investigate how global interconnectedness both enables more effective compliance with international obligations and creates new areas of obligation

response_modes.reason: Students need to distinguish between different types of 'issues' — legal uncertainty, political resistance, implementation gaps, and enforcement limits are all different. Structure the analysis to keep these categories clear.
The First Nations reconciliation/sovereignty direction connects international obligations to domestic civic life in a concrete way that makes the abstract enforcement problem tangible.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations reconciliation and sovereignty direction is substantively rich — it is not just another treaty-compliance case but raises questions about what justice requires beyond legal minimums, which is the deeper civic question this descriptor is building toward.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one issue in the application of Australia's international legal obligations
Explains why the issue arises, including at least one factor creating the tension or gap
Connects the analysis to a specific treaty or obligation
